payload.prompt: What makes a rush dangerous?

options.text: The puck is moving down the ice toward the opponent's zone with speed and numbers.
The goalie is pulled for an extra attacker.
options.explanation: That is an empty net, not a rush. A rush is a fast attack with the goalie in place.

options.text: Players are standing still waiting for a pass.
options.explanation: A rush is the opposite: fast movement up ice toward the net.

explanation.correct: Right. A rush is a fast break with numbers advantage or equal numbers moving toward the net.
explanation.incorrect: A rush is a high-speed attack from the neutral zone. It creates scoring chances because defenders are back.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rush starts in the neutral zone and ends at the net or defense.

payload.prompt: Tap where a rush begins.

diagram.alt: Hockey rink from above: defensive zone at bottom, center line in middle, offensive zone at top.

explanation.correct: Right. A rush starts in the neutral zone when players gain the puck and push up ice.
explanation.incorrect: A rush begins when a team gains possession and pushes toward the opponent's goal. The neutral zone is where the rush starts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rushes start in the neutral zone, end at the net.

payload.prompt: What is a 2-on-1 rush?

options.text: Two attacking players versus one defenseman: a numerical advantage that is dangerous because the defender cannot stop both.
options.explanation: Correct. A 2-on-1 is the most common odd-man rush and creates a high-scoring chance.

options.text: Two players shooting and one goalie saving.
One forward and two defensemen fighting for the puck.

explanation.correct: Right. A 2-on-1 gives the attackers the advantage: one can shoot, one can pass, and the lone defender cannot be in two places.
explanation.incorrect: A 2-on-1 is attackers outnumbering the defense. It is called an odd-man rush because the attackers have the numbers.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2-on-1 is two attackers against one defenseman: a scoring chance.

payload.prompt: A 3-on-2 rush is less dangerous than a 2-on-1. True or false?

scene.alt: Three attackers moving up ice against two defensemen.

explanation.correct: False. A 3-on-2 is even more dangerous than a 2-on-1 because the defensemen are more spread out and cannot help each other.
explanation.incorrect: A 3-on-2 is a high-danger rush. More attackers mean more options and less defense, so it is very dangerous.
explanation.sayThisLine: 3-on-2 and 2-on-1 both create elite scoring chances.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of defensive rush technique.
payload.template: A defenseman with {{control}} stops the rush early by closing the {{distance}} before the attacker can shoot or create a pass.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Tight gap control cuts down the attacker's time and options. The defender takes away space early.
explanation.incorrect: Tight gap means the defenseman stays close to the puck carrier. A loose gap gives too much space and allows a shot.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Pressure the opponent in their own zone to force turnovers and stop them from building a play.
Forwards hustle back into their own zone after a turnover to help defend the rush.
One forward deep in the opponent's zone, two covering the middle, two defensemen behind them.

explanation.summary: Forecheck is offense turning into defense. Backcheck is forwards getting back. Both stop scoring chances.
explanation.sayThisLine: Good forechecks force mistakes. Good backchecks stop breakaways.

payload.prompt: Which zone are these forwards forechecking in?

image.alt: Three attacking forwards (light color) pressing defenders (dark color) who are trying to move the puck out of their zone.

options.text: The offensive zone (opponent's zone)
options.explanation: Correct. Forechecking means attacking in the opponent's zone to disrupt their breakout.

options.text: The neutral zone
Their own defensive zone
options.explanation: Forechecking is in the opponent's zone. Defense in your own zone is not a forecheck.

explanation.correct: Right. Forechecking is the attacking team's offense becoming defense by pressuring in the opponent's zone.
explanation.incorrect: Forecheck means attacking in the opponent's zone. It is aggressive defense that forces turnovers.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forecheck = attack in their zone to get the puck back.

cues: Forechecking happens in the opponent's defensive zone
The goal is to force a turnover or bad pass
It is active pressure, not passive waiting

payload.prompt: What is the job of the deep forechecker in a 1-2-2 system?

options.text: Attack the puck carrier immediately and force them to pass or shoot quickly under pressure.
options.explanation: Correct. The deep forechecker is aggressive and creates the first line of pressure.

options.text: Stand in the blue line and wait for the puck.
Skate to the offensive zone and score a goal.

explanation.correct: Right. The deep forechecker is the most aggressive and forces the first mistake or bad decision.
explanation.incorrect: Forechecking requires aggression. The deep forechecker hunts the puck and the player with it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Deep forechecker: first line of attack, forces the first pass.

payload.prompt: Order how a forecheck reads the opponent's breakout.

items.text: The attacking team gains the puck or opponent has it in their zone.
items.why: Forechecking starts when you attack in the opponent's zone.

items.text: The deep forechecker attacks the puck carrier immediately.
items.why: First pressure forces the opponent to react under duress.

items.text: The second and third forecheckers cover the passing lanes.
items.why: Cut off pass options; force a worse decision.

items.text: The opponent forces a turnover or a weak breakout pass.
items.why: Good forecheck leads to a turnover or an easy reentry.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is how a forecheck builds pressure and forces mistakes.
explanation.incorrect: Forecheck starts with aggressive pressure, moves to cutting lanes, and ends in a turnover.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forecheck: pressure first, cut lanes second, force mistakes third.

payload.prompt: A good forecheck can tire the opponent's defense because they have less time to rest. True or false?

scene.alt: Attacking forwards pressuring the opponent's defensemen in their own zone.

explanation.correct: True. An aggressive forecheck prevents the opponent from regrouping and forces hurried decisions. It is both physical and mental pressure.
explanation.incorrect: A good forecheck is exhausting because defenders cannot rest and must deal with constant pressure.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forecheck = tired opponent = forced mistakes.

lessons.title: Read the forecheck and break out

payload.prompt: You are in your defensive zone with the puck. One forechecker is attacking you, two more are covering the wings, and your teammates are open. What do you do?
payload.scenario: Deep forechecker closing on you fast. Winger open along the boards. Center open in the neutral zone.

options.text: Pass to the winger along the boards to start the breakout.
options.consequence: Good choice. A wall pass move or quick flip gets the puck moving forward and lets your winger carry it out.

options.text: Shoot it up to the center in the neutral zone immediately.
options.consequence: Risky. The forechecker may intercept. Better to make a short pass first and have your winger carry it.

options.text: Skate backward and wait for the forechecker to get closer.
options.consequence: Bad idea. You lose space and time. A quick pass or move gets the puck away from pressure.

explanation.correct: Right. Short passes under pressure are safer than long passes. Get the puck to a moving player.
explanation.incorrect: A breakout under pressure needs a quick decision. Passing to an open player close to you is faster than a long pass.
explanation.sayThisLine: Under pressure, move it quick and short: to a teammate close by.

payload.prompt: Match the breakout type to how it works.

pairs.definition: Pass to a teammate along the boards who sends it back; simple and quick.
One defenseman passes behind the net to the partner, who exits with the puck.
A long pass from the defensive zone to a forward past the blue line.

explanation.summary: Breakouts have different risks and rewards. Short passes are safe; long passes are risky but fast.
explanation.sayThisLine: Safe breakout = short pass. Fast breakout = stretch pass.

payload.prompt: What should a defenseman avoid under forecheck pressure?

options.text: Holding the puck too long and letting the forechecker get closer.
options.explanation: Correct. Possession under pressure is risky; move it quickly.

options.text: Passing to a teammate at all.
Shooting the puck down the ice.

explanation.correct: Right. The longer you hold it, the more pressure builds. Quick decisions and fast hands beat forechecks.
explanation.incorrect: Under forecheck pressure, speed is everything. Get the puck moving before pressure gets too close.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pressure = move fast. Hold it = bad decision likely.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of a smart breakout.
payload.template: A smart breakout gets the puck {{direction}} by using {{method}} and avoids {{risk}}.

options: a wall pass or quick pass
gaps.correct: a wall pass or quick pass

explanation.correct: Exactly. A good breakout moves the puck up and out quickly, minimizing the chance of a turnover.
explanation.incorrect: Breakouts need speed and smart passing. Get out of your zone before pressure builds.

payload.prompt: When a forecheck forces a turnover in your defensive zone, your forwards should backcheck immediately. True or false?

scene.alt: Forwards backchecking quickly after a turnover in the defensive zone.

explanation.correct: True. A turnover means the other team has the puck. Fast backchecking stops them from scoring off the turnover.
explanation.incorrect: A quick backcheck after a turnover prevents the opponent from scoring. Fast transitions are won by quick feet.
explanation.sayThisLine: Backcheck fast after a turnover; stop the breakaway.

lessons.title: Neutral zone and the trap
lessons.objective: Explain how teams defend the middle.

payload.prompt: What is the neutral-zone trap?

options.text: A defensive system that clogs the middle of the ice to force turnovers and slow the game down.
options.explanation: Correct. The trap is a passive, defensive strategy that is effective but not always entertaining.

options.text: An offensive strategy to score goals.
A penalty for too many men on the ice.

explanation.correct: Right. The trap stops the rush by packing defenders into the neutral zone. Teams hate playing against it.
explanation.incorrect: The neutral-zone trap is defensive. It fills the neutral zone with players to stop the other team from gaining speed.
explanation.sayThisLine: Trap = fill the middle, force a turnover, slow the game.

payload.prompt: The trap is most effective against teams that want to play a fast, up-tempo style. True or false?

scene.alt: Defenders filling the neutral zone, forcing the puck carrier to slow down or dump the puck.

explanation.correct: True. The trap slows the game and takes away space, which frustrates fast-paced teams.
explanation.incorrect: The trap is designed to slow play and neutralize speed. It is most effective against high-tempo offenses.
explanation.sayThisLine: Trap kills speed; speed kills the trap.

payload.prompt: What is the difference between a carry-in and a dump-in?

options.text: A carry-in is when the puck is brought over the line with possession; a dump-in is when it is shot in without control.
options.explanation: Correct. Carry-ins create more chances but are riskier against a good trap.

options.text: A carry-in is shooting the puck; a dump-in is passing.
They are the same thing with different names.

explanation.correct: Right. Carry-ins are aggressive and create better offensive chances. Dump-ins are conservative but safer.
explanation.incorrect: Zone entry is about puck control. Carrying it in is better for offense; dumping is safer but gives up possession.
explanation.sayThisLine: Carry-in = control, better chances. Dump-in = safe, risky to recover.

payload.prompt: You are on offense. The other team is playing a tight neutral-zone trap. How do you enter their zone?
payload.scenario: The neutral zone is packed with defenders. Your team has the puck at center ice. You have a fast winger and a playmaking center.

options.text: Send the winger in fast with the puck to carry it through the trap.
options.consequence: High risk. The trap is designed to stop rushes. Speed alone may not work.

options.text: Dump the puck behind the net and chase it for possession.
options.consequence: Safe and effective. Gets into the zone with possession, avoiding the trap.

options.text: Pass back to the defenseman and try again.
options.consequence: Just delays the problem. You need to enter the zone eventually.

explanation.correct: Right. Against a trap, dumping and chasing gives you possession and avoids the neutral-zone kill.
explanation.incorrect: The trap kills speed entries. Dump-and-chase is the classic counter to a neutral-zone trap.
explanation.sayThisLine: Against the trap: dump, chase, cycle. Speed dies in the trap.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of a neutral-zone trap.

options: packing the neutral zone with players
gaps.correct: packing the neutral zone with players

explanation.correct: Exactly. The trap is a defensive strategy that reduces pace and forces bad plays.
explanation.incorrect: Trap strategy: fill the middle, stop the rush, force turnovers in the neutral zone.

payload.prompt: Match the offensive concept to what it means.

pairs.definition: Pass the puck around the boards in the offensive zone to tire the defense and set up a scoring chance.
Shoot the puck into the opponent's zone and chase it for possession, then regroup.
Skate the puck over the blue line into the opponent's zone with possession, looking for an immediate scoring chance.

explanation.summary: Each entry strategy has a purpose. Cycles tire the defense. Dump-and-chase is safe. Carry-ins are aggressive.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cycle for chances, dump for possession, carry for speed.

payload.prompt: A cycle can last for a full minute or more without a shot. True or false?

scene.alt: Three forwards passing along the boards in the offensive zone, wearing down the defense.

explanation.correct: True. A cycle is a patient, physical game that tires defenders and waits for a breakdown.
explanation.incorrect: Long cycles are common; teams use them to control play and wait for an opening.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cycle = possession, patience, and wearing down the defense.

payload.prompt: What is the biggest risk of a dump-and-chase?

options.text: The defending team gets to the puck first and starts a breakout.
options.explanation: Correct. If the defending team wins the race, they have an odd-man rush opportunity.

options.text: The puck bounces off the goalie.
The puck goes out of play.

explanation.correct: Right. A dump-and-chase is a numbers game. You have to win the race to get the puck back.
explanation.incorrect: Dump-and-chase gives possession control to whoever reaches the puck first. Speed matters.
explanation.sayThisLine: Dump-and-chase is a race: first to the puck wins.

payload.prompt: Order how a cycle works in the offensive zone.

items.text: The team enters the offensive zone with possession.
items.why: Cycling happens when you control the puck in the attacking zone.

items.text: Players pass along the boards or in circles, moving the puck constantly.
items.why: Constant motion tires the defense and creates space.

items.text: The defense gets fatigued and loses structure.
items.why: Chasing the puck for a minute or more is exhausting.

items.text: A breakdown in defense creates a scoring chance.
items.why: Tired, disorganized defense allows a shot or pass to the slot.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is how cycles work: possession, motion, fatigue, breakdown, goal.
explanation.incorrect: A cycle is patient offense that wears down defense until a chance appears.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cycle long enough and defense gets tired.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of dump-and-chase strategy.
payload.template: A dump-and-chase puts the puck {{location}} and the attacking team {{action}}, {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Dump-and-chase is a race for possession deep in the zone.
explanation.incorrect: Dump-and-chase means shooting deep and chasing it quickly to create a numbers advantage if you get there first.

payload.prompt: Tap the slot, the high-danger scoring area.

diagram.alt: Hockey rink from above, focusing on the offensive zone with the goal area.

explanation.correct: Right. The slot is where most goals come from. Goals from the slot go in far more often than from the perimeter.
explanation.incorrect: The slot is the area between the faceoff circles in front of the net. That is the danger zone for scoring.
explanation.sayThisLine: Slot = high-danger area. Goals come from the slot.

payload.prompt: What does it mean to screen the goalie?

options.text: Stand in front of the goalie to block the view and hide the shot.
options.explanation: Correct. A screen makes it hard for the goalie to see and react to a shot.

options.text: Check the goalie into the boards.
Pass the puck to the goalie's side.

explanation.correct: Right. A screen is a smart offensive move that takes away the goalie's view.
explanation.incorrect: A screen means an offensive player stands in the goalie's sight line, making saves harder.
explanation.sayThisLine: Screen = block the goalie's view. A screen helps even weak shots go in.

payload.prompt: A tip redirects a shot by having a player touch it with their stick as it passes in front of the net. True or false?

scene.alt: A forward redirecting a point shot with their stick in front of the net.

explanation.correct: True. A tip changes the puck's direction and speed, and the goalie cannot react fast enough.
explanation.incorrect: A tip is a redirect; the player touches the shot to change its path. Tips create goals.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tip = touch it, redirect it, score it.

payload.prompt: What is a one-timer?

options.text: A shot taken immediately off a pass, without stopping the puck first.
options.explanation: Correct. One-timers are fast and dangerous because the goalie has no time to react.

options.text: A shot that only counts once per game.
Stopping the puck and then shooting.

explanation.correct: Right. One-timers are quick; the goalie sees the pass and the shot arrives before they can set.
explanation.incorrect: A one-timer is a direct shot from a pass. It is a power-play weapon.
explanation.sayThisLine: One-timer = fast release. Goalie has no time.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of a high-danger scoring play.
payload.template: A goal is most likely when a shot comes from the {{area}}, helped by {{tactic}}, and {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Slot shots with help (screens or tips) are the highest-percentage goals.
explanation.incorrect: Scoring comes from the slot. Help from screens and tips increases the chance even more.

payload.prompt: Which formation is this power play using?

image.alt: Five forwards arranged: one at the point (top), three across the middle (umbrella shape), one at the net (low slot).

options.text: 1-3-1 (one point, three middle, one net)
options.explanation: Correct. The 1-3-1 spreads the defense across the ice.

options.text: Umbrella (three across the top)
options.explanation: The umbrella has three players at the top; this has one at the point and three in the middle.

options.text: Overload (numbers on one side)
options.explanation: An overload puts more players on one side of the ice. This formation is balanced.

explanation.correct: Right. The 1-3-1 puts a defenseman at the point and spreads the forwards to create shooting lanes.
explanation.incorrect: The 1-3-1 has one at the top, three in the middle, and one low. It opens up the middle for one-timers.
explanation.sayThisLine: 1-3-1 opens lanes. Umbrella spreads the top. Overload stacks one side.

cues: Count the players at each level
1-3-1 has one high, three middle, one low
Umbrella has three across the top

payload.prompt: Match the power play formation to its purpose.

pairs.definition: One defenseman at the point, three forwards across the middle, one at the net. Creates one-timer opportunities.
Three forwards across the top of the zone, one at the net, one defenseman. Spreads the penalty kill.
More players on one side of the ice than the other. Exploits a weak side of the kill.

explanation.summary: Each formation has a different strength. Teams switch to find what works against a defense.
explanation.sayThisLine: 1-3-1 for tips, umbrella for space, overload for a weak side.

payload.prompt: Why is the 1-3-1 so effective at setting up one-timers?

options.text: The three forwards in the middle create passing lanes where one can shoot without stopping the puck.
options.explanation: Correct. The 1-3-1 is built around one-timer chances from the middle.

options.text: The defenseman at the point always scores.
It takes more time than other formations.

explanation.correct: Right. The 1-3-1 creates the most one-timer opportunities because of the middle spacing.
explanation.incorrect: The 1-3-1 is a one-timer machine. The three-forward middle enables quick, hard shots.
explanation.sayThisLine: 1-3-1 = one-timer city.

payload.prompt: The umbrella formation is more aggressive than the 1-3-1. True or false?

scene.alt: Five players spread across the offensive zone in an umbrella shape.

explanation.correct: False. The umbrella is more about spreading the defense and creating space. The 1-3-1 is more aggressive for tips and one-timers.
explanation.incorrect: The 1-3-1 is the more aggressive, scoring-focused formation. Umbrella is more spread-out.
explanation.sayThisLine: 1-3-1 = aggressive tips. Umbrella = space and cycling.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of power play formations.
payload.template: A power play formation {{goal}} by {{method}} and creates {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Power play formations overload or stretch the defense to create scoring opportunities.
explanation.incorrect: Formations spread the kill and create space or shot lanes. Each formation targets different weaknesses.

lessons.title: Find the seam on the power play
lessons.objective: Spot the open pass against a box.

payload.prompt: You are on the power play against a box penalty-kill formation. Find the passing lane and score.
The penalty kill is in a box: four players forming a square. Your power play is in a 1-3-1. Where is the open passing lane?
payload.scenario: Defenseman at the point with the puck. Three forwards in the middle. One forward at the net. Box is tight. One seam is visible.

options.text: Between the left and right forwards in the middle, a passing lane to the net.
options.consequence: Good read. That seam is open; one-timer chance at the net.

options.text: Around the boards to the winger.
options.consequence: That side is covered by the box. Better to find the middle seam.

options.text: Shoot from the point right through the box.
options.consequence: The box is designed to block that. Pass first, shoot second.

explanation.correct: Right. The box has seams; find them with quick passes.
explanation.incorrect: A box kill has openings. The middle seams are the target for a 1-3-1.
explanation.sayThisLine: Box has seams. Find them, pass, one-timer.

payload.prompt: What is the penalty kill's box formation designed to do?

options.text: Block the high-danger area and force the other team to pass around the perimeter.
options.explanation: Correct. The box protects the slot and forces outside passing.

options.text: Score a goal.
Tire the power play with constant pressure.

explanation.correct: Right. The box is a fortress that protects the net and forces the power play to the perimeter.
explanation.incorrect: The box kill defends the slot. It makes the power play work for their chances.
explanation.sayThisLine: Box = protect the middle, force the outside.

payload.prompt: A seam in the penalty kill is an open passing lane where a defender is out of position. True or false?

scene.alt: A passing lane opening up through a box formation as players move.

explanation.correct: True. Seams appear when the box shifts or a defender moves. Quick passes exploit them.
explanation.incorrect: A seam is a gap in the kill formation. Fast passes find seams and create goals.
explanation.sayThisLine: Find the seam, pass it, shoot it, score it.

payload.prompt: Order how a power play beats a box formation.

items.text: The power play spreads the box with movement and passing.
items.why: Movement tires and shifts the box, creating seams.

items.text: A seam opens when the box moves or a defender loses position.
items.why: Constant motion creates gaps in the kill.

items.text: A quick pass exploits the seam before the box can reset.
items.why: Timing is everything; the pass must be fast.

items.text: A shot (often a one-timer) finishes the chance.
items.why: A shot from the seam is high-danger.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is how power plays work: move, find seams, pass, shoot.
explanation.incorrect: Power play strategy: movement, seam-finding, quick passing, hard shot.
explanation.sayThisLine: PP = move, seam, pass, goal.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of finding a seam on the power play.
payload.template: A seam appears when {{trigger}}, and the power play exploits it with {{action}}, resulting in {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Seams are fleeting; quick execution capitalizes on them.
explanation.incorrect: Finding seams requires constant motion and quick decisions. Speed matters.

lessons.title: Who has the point? D-zone coverage
lessons.objective: Assign coverage in the defensive zone.

payload.prompt: You are on defense. Assign coverage in the zone. Mark the opponent's best players and control the scoring areas.
Three forwards are in your defensive zone attacking the net. One is at the point, one in the slot, one on the wing. You have three defensemen. How do you cover?
payload.scenario: Opponent has possession at the top. One forward in slot is dangerous. One on wing. One at point shooting from distance.

options.text: One defender on the slot (most dangerous), one on the wing, one watches the point.
options.consequence: Perfect. Mark the slot player tight, cover the wings, watch perimeter threats.

options.text: All three defenders stay deep by the goal.
Two on the point, one in the slot.

explanation.correct: Right. Cover the danger areas. Slot is highest risk.
explanation.incorrect: Coverage priorities: slot player first, wings second, point third.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cover the slot tight, watch the wings, eyes on the point.

payload.prompt: What is the difference between man-to-man and zone coverage in the defensive zone?

options.text: Man-to-man assigns each defender to an opponent; zone has each defender cover an area.
options.explanation: Correct. Man-to-man follows players; zone covers space.

options.text: Man-to-man is always better.
They are the same thing.

explanation.correct: Right. Man-to-man is tight; zone is flexible. Teams use both depending on the situation.
explanation.incorrect: Man-to-man = follow a player. Zone = cover an area. Each has strengths.
explanation.sayThisLine: Man = follow, zone = space. Pick the right one.

payload.prompt: In zone coverage, a defender collapses toward the goal if the puck is in that area, leaving the perimeter open. True or false?

scene.alt: Defenders collapsing toward the net, leaving the perimeter open.

explanation.correct: True. Zone coverage means protecting the center and goal, which sometimes leaves the perimeter open for outside shots.
explanation.incorrect: Zone coverage protects the slot but can leave perimeter shots open; that is the trade-off.
explanation.sayThisLine: Zone = protect the middle, watch the perimeter.

payload.prompt: Match the coverage style to its description.

pairs.definition: Each defender is assigned to an opponent. If the opponent moves, the defender follows.
Each defender covers an area. If an opponent enters, the defender challenges them.
All defenders pack around the net to block shots. Risk: perimeter shots go in.

explanation.summary: Coverage styles have different risks and rewards. Smart teams switch based on the situation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Man is tight. Zone is flexible. Collapse is risky but protects the center.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of defensive-zone coverage.
payload.template: In the defensive zone, a team uses {{method}} coverage by {{action}} and {{goal}}.

options: protecting the net and stopping chances
gaps.correct: protecting the net and stopping chances

explanation.correct: Exactly. Coverage is about assigning responsibility to stop scoring chances.
explanation.incorrect: Coverage strategies assign each defender a job: follow a player or cover space, then stop the opponent's chance.
